#!/bin/bash
# Demo: LED blink program showing LED toggling and UART output
# Runs led_blink.lgo which blinks LED D2 five times, printing 'L' each toggle
set -e

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
PROJECT_DIR="$(cd "$SCRIPT_DIR/.." && pwd)"

# Build the debugger
echo "=== Building cor24-dbg ==="
cargo build -p cor24-cli --manifest-path "$PROJECT_DIR/Cargo.toml" 2>&1
DBG="$PROJECT_DIR/target/debug/cor24-dbg"
LGO="$PROJECT_DIR/tests/programs/led_blink.lgo"

echo ""
echo "=== Running LED Blink Demo ==="
echo "Program: led_blink.s -> blinks LED D2 five times, prints 'L' each toggle"
echo ""

# Feed commands via stdin
$DBG "$LGO" <<'EOF'
disas 0 20
led
step 100
led
step 100
led
run 100000
uart
led
quit
EOF

cor24-emu: COR24 emulator (runtime only — use cor24-asm to assemble)

Usage:
  cor24-emu --demo [options]                    Run built-in LED demo
  cor24-emu --lgo <file.lgo> [opts]             Run a pre-built .lgo
  cor24-emu --load-binary <f>@<a> --entry <a>   Run a raw-binary image

Options:
  -h                     Short help (this message)
  --help                 Extended help with AI agent guidance
  -V, --version          Version, copyright, license, build info
  --speed, -s <ips>      Instructions per second (default: 100000)
  --time, -t <secs>      Time limit in seconds (default: 10)
  --max-instructions, -n <count>  Stop after N instructions (-1 = no limit)
  --uart-input, -u <str> Send characters to UART RX (supports \n, \x21)
  --uart-file <path>     Read file contents into UART RX buffer (appends 0x04 EOF)
  --quiet, -q            UART TX as plain text on stdout; logs to stderr
  --entry, -e <label|addr> Set entry point (numeric address only)
  --dump                 Dump CPU state, I/O, and non-zero memory after halt
  --dump-uart            Show UART transaction log (chronological IN/OUT)
  --dump-i2c             Show I2C transaction log (chronological START/byte/STOP)
  --i2c-device <spec>    Attach an I2C device (repeatable). Specs:
                           add1@<addr>[?wrap=<n>]   universal +1 test slave
                           tmp101@<addr>[?temp=<f>][?config=<n>]  TI temp sensor
  --trace <N>            Dump last N instructions on halt/timeout (default: 50)
  --step                 Print each instruction as it executes
  --terminal             Bridge stdin/stdout to UART (interactive mode)
  --echo                 Local echo in terminal mode (for programs that don't echo)
  --load-binary <file>@<addr>  Load raw bytes into memory at address
  --patch <addr>=<value> Write 24-bit value to memory (repeatable)
  --stack-kilobytes <3|8>  EBR stack size (default: 3, max: 8)
  --switch <on|off>      Set button S2 state (default: off/released)
  --uart-never-ready     UART TX stays busy forever (test polling)
  --guard-jumps          Halt if PC leaves the code region (catches bad control flow)
  --code-end <addr>      Upper bound for --guard-jumps (default: program_end)
  --canary <addr>[=val]  Halt if memory at addr changes (default magic: 0xDEADBE)
  --watch-range <lo> <hi> Halt if any byte in [lo, hi] changes (repeatable)

Examples:
  cor24-emu --demo --speed 100000 --time 10
  cor24-asm prog.s -o prog.lgo && cor24-emu --lgo prog.lgo --dump --speed 0
  cor24-emu --lgo echo.lgo -u 'abc!' --speed 0 --dump --dump-uart
  cor24-emu --lgo repl.lgo --terminal --echo --speed 0
  cor24-emu --lgo pvm.lgo --load-binary hello.p24@0x010000 --terminal
  cor24-emu --load-binary pvm.bin@0 --load-binary hello.p24@0x010000 --entry 0 --terminal
  cor24-emu --load-binary pvm.bin@0 --patch 0x09D7=0x010000 --entry 0 --terminal
  cor24-emu --lgo examples/i2c/tmp101/tmp101.lgo --i2c-device tmp101@0x4A?temp=25.0 \
                 -n 200000 --quiet --dump-i2c

=== Extended Help ===

COR24 Architecture:
  24-bit RISC CPU (C-Oriented RISC) designed for embedded systems education.
  3 general-purpose registers (r0, r1, r2), frame pointer (fp), stack pointer (sp).
  Variable-length instructions (1/2/4 bytes). 24-bit address space (16 MB).

Memory Map:
  000000-0FFFFF  SRAM (1 MB) — code and data
  FEE000-FEFFFF  EBR (8 KB) — stack (3 KB default, 8 KB with --stack-kilobytes 8)
  FF0000-FFFFFF  I/O — LED/switch at FF0000, UART at FF0100-FF0101

# makerlisp blinky_s2 — D2 follows S2

A 27-byte COR24 program from the MakerLisp/COR24-TB world: hold down
button **S2** and LED **D2** lights up; release **S2** and **D2** goes
dark. The whole thing fits in three lines of `.lgo`.

## The program

`tests/programs/blinky_s2.lgo`:

```
L000000807F7E652B0000FF2E00820013F82900ECFE662A00E0FEC7000000
; Blinky - D2 LED follows S2 button press
G00000E
```

- `L000000…` — one load record: 27 bytes starting at address `0x000000`.
- `;` — comment.
- `G00000E` — start execution at `0x00000E`.

## Disassembly

```
; --- loop body (entered via call from startup) ---
000000: 80           push fp
000001: 7F           push r2
000002: 7E           push r1
000003: 65           mov  fp,sp
000004: 2B 00 00 FF  la   r2,0xFF0000   ; r2 = IO_LEDSWDAT
000008: 2E 00        lb   r0,(r2)       ; r0 = switch byte (bit 0 = S2)
00000A: 82 00        sb   r0,(r2)       ; write same byte -> drives LED D2
00000C: 13 F8        bra  0x000008      ; forever

; --- entry point (G00000E) ---
00000E: 29 00 EC FE  la   r0,0xFEEC00   ; top of EBR stack
000012: 66           mov  sp,r0         ; sp = 0xFEEC00
000013: 2A 00 E0 FE  la   r1,0xFEE000   ; r1 = bottom of EBR
000017: C7 00 00 00  call 0x000000      ; jump into the loop (never returns)
```

Reproduce with `cor24-dbg`:

```bash
./target/debug/cor24-dbg tests/programs/blinky_s2.lgo <<<'disas 0 30'
```

## Analysis

`IO_LEDSWDAT` at `0xFF0000` is the trick: bit 0 of the **same byte** is
**S2 on read** and **D2 on write** (both active-low — `1` = released /
off, `0` = pressed / on). The loop is therefore three instructions:

1. `lb r0,(r2)` — read S2 into bit 0 of `r0`.
2. `sb r0,(r2)` — write that bit back, so D2 mirrors S2.
3. `bra 0x000008` — spin.

Startup at `0x0E` sets `sp` to the top of EBR (`0xFEEC00`), parks `r1`
at the bottom of EBR (`0xFEE000` — bookkeeping the program never uses
again), and `call`s into the loop. The prologue at `0x00`
(`push fp / push r2 / push r1 / mov fp,sp`) burns three slots of stack
and is never unwound; that's fine because the loop never returns.

Anything past `0x1B` reads as `0x00` (`add r0,r0`) but is never executed.

## Testing

### 1. S2 released (default)

```bash
./target/debug/cor24-emu --lgo tests/programs/blinky_s2.lgo \
  --time 1 --speed 100000 --dump 2>&1 | tail -5
```

Expect `LED D2: 0x01  off`.

### 2. S2 pressed at boot

The `--switch on` flag pins S2 low for the whole run:

```bash
./target/debug/cor24-emu --lgo tests/programs/blinky_s2.lgo \
  --switch on --time 1 --speed 100000 --dump 2>&1 | tail -5
```

Expect `LED D2: 0x00  on`.

> Caveat: the `--dump` output's `BTN S2:` field reflects the raw
> `io.switches` register, which the dump rendering reports as
> "released" because the program last *wrote* the LED side of the
> shared address. Trust `LED D2:` for the actual driven output.

### 3. Toggle S2 in a loop (integration test)

The CLI takes a single `--switch` value at start-up, so for a live
toggle we drive the emulator from Rust. The test in
`tests/integration_tests.rs` (`test_blinky_s2_led_follows_switch`)
does this directly:

```rust
let executor = Executor::new();
executor.run(&mut cpu, 50); // run startup + a few loop iterations

for cycle in 0..5 {
    cpu.io.switches = 0x00;       // press S2
    executor.run(&mut cpu, 30);
    assert_eq!(cpu.io.leds, 0x00, "cycle {cycle}: D2 should be on");

    cpu.io.switches = 0x01;       // release S2
    executor.run(&mut cpu, 30);
    assert_eq!(cpu.io.leds, 0x01, "cycle {cycle}: D2 should be off");
}
```

Run just this test:

```bash
cargo test --test integration_tests test_blinky_s2_led_follows_switch
```

Or the whole workspace:

```bash
cargo test --workspace
```

#!/bin/bash
# Demo: Hello World UART output
#
# Assembles and runs hello_world.s, capturing UART output to a shell variable.
# Shows the full pipeline: .s source → .lgo binary → emulator → UART output
set -e

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
PROJECT_DIR="$(cd "$SCRIPT_DIR/.." && pwd)"
DBG="$PROJECT_DIR/target/debug/cor24-dbg"
LGO="$PROJECT_DIR/tests/programs/hello_world.lgo"
SRC="$PROJECT_DIR/tests/programs/hello_world.s"

# Build the debugger
echo "=== Building cor24-dbg ==="
cargo build -p cor24-cli --manifest-path "$PROJECT_DIR/Cargo.toml" 2>&1

echo ""
echo "=== Source: hello_world.s ==="
cat "$SRC"

echo ""
echo "=== Running in emulator ==="
echo ""

# Run the debugger, capture full output
RAW_OUTPUT=$($DBG "$LGO" <<'CMDS'
run 1000
uart
quit
CMDS
)

echo "$RAW_OUTPUT"

echo ""
echo "=== Extracting UART output into shell variable ==="
echo ""

# Extract UART content: everything between "UART output buffer..." line and next "(cor24)" prompt
# The UART output appears on lines after the "UART output buffer (N chars):" header
UART_OUTPUT=$(echo "$RAW_OUTPUT" | awk '/UART output buffer/{found=1; next} found && /[(]cor24[)]/{found=0} found && NF{print}')

echo "UART_OUTPUT variable contains:"
echo "---"
echo "$UART_OUTPUT"
echo "---"
echo ""

# Verify the output
EXPECTED="Hello, World!"
if echo "$UART_OUTPUT" | grep -qF "$EXPECTED"; then
    echo "PASS: UART output contains '$EXPECTED'"
else
    echo "FAIL: Expected '$EXPECTED' in UART output"
    exit 1
fi

echo ""
echo "=== Using UART output in a pipeline ==="
echo ""

# Demonstrate piping UART output
CHAR_COUNT=$(echo -n "$UART_OUTPUT" | wc -c)
WORD_COUNT=$(echo "$UART_OUTPUT" | wc -w)
echo "Character count: $CHAR_COUNT"
echo "Word count: $WORD_COUNT"
echo "Uppercase: $(echo "$UART_OUTPUT" | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]')"
echo "Hex dump:"
echo -n "$UART_OUTPUT" | xxd | head -3

# Demo: Count down from 5 to 1 with UART output and breakpoint debugging

set -e

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
PROJECT_DIR="$(cd "$SCRIPT_DIR/.." && pwd)"

# Build the debugger
echo "=== Building cor24-dbg ==="
cargo build -p cor24-cli --manifest-path "$PROJECT_DIR/Cargo.toml" 2>&1
DBG="$PROJECT_DIR/target/debug/cor24-dbg"
LGO="$PROJECT_DIR/tests/programs/count_down.lgo"

echo ""
echo "=== Running Count Down Demo ==="

echo ""

$DBG "$LGO" <<'EOF'
disas 0 14
break 0x0B
run
info
print r1
continue
delete all
run
uart
quit
EOF

# Demo: Blinky-S2 — LED D2 mirrors button S2
# Runs blinky_s2.lgo with S2 released (default) and pressed, dumping
# the LED/switch I/O register each time so you can see D2 follow S2.
#
# Toggling S2 *during* execution is exercised by the integration test
# `test_blinky_s2_led_follows_switch` (see tests/integration_tests.rs).
set -e

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
PROJECT_DIR="$(cd "$SCRIPT_DIR/.." && pwd)"

echo "=== Building cor24-emu ==="
cargo build -p cor24-cli --manifest-path "$PROJECT_DIR/Cargo.toml" 2>&1
EMU="$PROJECT_DIR/target/debug/cor24-emu"
LGO="$PROJECT_DIR/tests/programs/blinky_s2.lgo"

run_case() {
    local label="$1"
    shift
    echo ""
    echo "=== $label ==="
    "$EMU" --lgo "$LGO" --time 1 --speed 100000 --dump "$@" 2>&1 \
        | grep -E "^  LED D2:|^  BTN S2:"
}

echo ""
echo "=== Program: blinky_s2.lgo (entry 0x0E) ==="
echo "    D2 follows S2: bit 0 of 0xFF0000 is switch on read, LED on write."
echo ""
cat "$LGO"

run_case "S2 released (default)"
run_case "S2 pressed (--switch on)" --switch on

echo ""
echo "=== Toggling S2 mid-run ==="
echo "The CLI takes a single --switch value at start-up. To toggle S2"
echo "during execution, run the integration test instead:"
echo ""
echo "    cargo test --test integration_tests test_blinky_s2_led_follows_switch"

# makerlisp blinky_s2 — D2 follows S2

A 27-byte COR24 program from the MakerLisp/COR24-TB world: hold down
button **S2** and LED **D2** lights up; release **S2** and **D2** goes
dark. The whole thing fits in three lines of `.lgo`.

## The program

`tests/programs/blinky_s2.lgo`:

```
L000000807F7E652B0000FF2E00820013F82900ECFE662A00E0FEC7000000
; Blinky - D2 LED follows S2 button press
G00000E
```

- `L000000…` — one load record: 27 bytes starting at address `0x000000`.
- `;` — comment.
- `G00000E` — start execution at `0x00000E`.

## Disassembly

```
; --- loop body (entered via call from startup) ---
000000: 80           push fp
000001: 7F           push r2
000002: 7E           push r1
000003: 65           mov  fp,sp
000004: 2B 00 00 FF  la   r2,0xFF0000   ; r2 = IO_LEDSWDAT
000008: 2E 00        lb   r0,(r2)       ; r0 = switch byte (bit 0 = S2)
00000A: 82 00        sb   r0,(r2)       ; write same byte -> drives LED D2
00000C: 13 F8        bra  0x000008      ; forever

; --- entry point (G00000E) ---
00000E: 29 00 EC FE  la   r0,0xFEEC00   ; top of EBR stack
000012: 66           mov  sp,r0         ; sp = 0xFEEC00
000013: 2A 00 E0 FE  la   r1,0xFEE000   ; r1 = bottom of EBR
000017: C7 00 00 00  call 0x000000      ; jump into the loop (never returns)
```

Reproduce with `cor24-dbg`:

```bash
./target/debug/cor24-dbg tests/programs/blinky_s2.lgo <<<'disas 0 30'
```

## Analysis

`IO_LEDSWDAT` at `0xFF0000` is the trick: bit 0 of the **same byte** is
**S2 on read** and **D2 on write** (both active-low — `1` = released /
off, `0` = pressed / on). The loop is therefore three instructions:

1. `lb r0,(r2)` — read S2 into bit 0 of `r0`.
2. `sb r0,(r2)` — write that bit back, so D2 mirrors S2.
3. `bra 0x000008` — spin.

Startup at `0x0E` sets `sp` to the top of EBR (`0xFEEC00`), parks `r1`
at the bottom of EBR (`0xFEE000` — bookkeeping the program never uses
again), and `call`s into the loop. The prologue at `0x00`
(`push fp / push r2 / push r1 / mov fp,sp`) burns three slots of stack
and is never unwound; that's fine because the loop never returns.

Anything past `0x1B` reads as `0x00` (`add r0,r0`) but is never executed.

## Testing

### 1. S2 released (default)

```bash
./target/debug/cor24-emu --lgo tests/programs/blinky_s2.lgo \
  --time 1 --speed 100000 --dump 2>&1 | tail -5
```

Expect `LED D2: 0x01  off`.

### 2. S2 pressed at boot

The `--switch on` flag pins S2 low for the whole run:

```bash
./target/debug/cor24-emu --lgo tests/programs/blinky_s2.lgo \
  --switch on --time 1 --speed 100000 --dump 2>&1 | tail -5
```

Expect `LED D2: 0x00  on`.

> Caveat: the `--dump` output's `BTN S2:` field reflects the raw
> `io.switches` register, which the dump rendering reports as
> "released" because the program last *wrote* the LED side of the
> shared address. Trust `LED D2:` for the actual driven output.

### 3. Toggle S2 in a loop (integration test)

The CLI takes a single `--switch` value at start-up, so for a live
toggle we drive the emulator from Rust. The test in
`tests/integration_tests.rs` (`test_blinky_s2_led_follows_switch`)
does this directly:

```rust
let executor = Executor::new();
executor.run(&mut cpu, 50); // run startup + a few loop iterations

for cycle in 0..5 {
    cpu.io.switches = 0x00;       // press S2
    executor.run(&mut cpu, 30);
    assert_eq!(cpu.io.leds, 0x00, "cycle {cycle}: D2 should be on");

    cpu.io.switches = 0x01;       // release S2
    executor.run(&mut cpu, 30);
    assert_eq!(cpu.io.leds, 0x01, "cycle {cycle}: D2 should be off");
}
```

Run just this test:

```bash
cargo test --test integration_tests test_blinky_s2_led_follows_switch
```

Or the whole workspace:

```bash
cargo test --workspace
```

# CLI demos

Each script in `scripts/demo-cli-*.sh` builds the CLI binaries and runs a
small program end-to-end. They double as sanity checks for the emulator
and as runnable references for new users.

All demos assume you are at the repo root. Each script handles its own
`cargo build`; you do not need to build first.

| Script | Program | What it shows |
|--------|---------|---------------|
| `demo-cli-hello-world.sh` | `tests/programs/hello_world.lgo` | UART string output; extracting UART text into a shell variable |
| `demo-cli-count-down.sh` | `tests/programs/count_down.lgo` | Breakpoints, single-stepping, register inspection in `cor24-dbg` |
| `demo-cli-led-blink.sh` | `tests/programs/led_blink.lgo` | LED toggling alongside UART output from a blink loop |
| `demo-cli-blinky-s2.sh` | `tests/programs/blinky_s2.lgo` | D2 LED mirrors S2 button via the shared `IO_LEDSWDAT` bit |
| `demo-cli-sieve.sh` | `docs/research/asld24/sieve.lgo` | Sieve of Eratosthenes benchmark (~500M instructions) |

## hello-world

```bash
scripts/demo-cli-hello-world.sh
```

Drives `cor24-dbg` against `hello_world.lgo`, captures the full debugger
session into `RAW_OUTPUT`, then uses `awk` to extract just the UART text
into `UART_OUTPUT`. Demonstrates the recommended pattern for using the
emulator in a shell pipeline (the same `awk` recipe is reproduced in
`docs/cli-emulator-guide.md`).

## count-down

```bash
scripts/demo-cli-count-down.sh
```

Runs `count_down.lgo` (prints `54321` to UART) through `cor24-dbg`:
disassemble, set a breakpoint at `0x0B`, run, inspect `r1`, continue,
clear breakpoints, run to completion, dump UART.

## led-blink

```bash
scripts/demo-cli-led-blink.sh
```

Runs `led_blink.lgo` — toggles LED D2 five times and prints `L` each
toggle. The script single-steps, samples the LED state with `led` between
chunks, and finally dumps UART. Useful for seeing the timing relationship
between an LED write and a UART transmit.

## blinky-s2

```bash

# MakerLisp COR24 CLI Emulator Guide

The `cor24-dbg` debugger lets you load, run, step through, and inspect
[MakerLisp](https://makerlisp.com) COR24 programs assembled with the
reference `as24` toolchain.

## Quick Start

### 1. Assemble a program

```bash
# Assemble and link into LGO format
cor24-as < tests/programs/hello_uart.s | longlgo > hello_uart.lgo

# View the listing to see addresses and opcodes
cor24-as -l < tests/programs/hello_uart.s
```

### 2. Run in the debugger

```bash
cor24-dbg hello_uart.lgo
```

If the program's entry point is not at address 0 (e.g. sieve.lgo has
`_main` at 0x93):

```bash
cor24-dbg --entry 0x93 docs/research/asld24/sieve.lgo
```

### 3. Debug

```
(cor24) run                  # run until halt/breakpoint/limit
(cor24) step                 # single step one instruction
(cor24) step 10              # step 10 instructions
(cor24) info                 # show all registers
(cor24) disas                # disassemble at PC
(cor24) x /16 0xFF0100       # examine 16 bytes at UART address
```

## Command Reference

| Command | Short | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| `run [N]` | `r` | Run N instructions (default 100M) |
| `step [N]` | `s` | Single step N instructions |
| `next` | `n` | Step over (skip into jal calls) |
| `continue` | `c` | Continue from breakpoint |
| `break <addr>` | `b` | Set breakpoint at address |
| `delete <N\|all>` | `d` | Delete breakpoint(s) |
| `info [r\|b]` | `i` | Show registers or breakpoints |
| `examine [/N] <addr>` | `x` | Examine N bytes at address |
| `print <reg\|addr>` | `p` | Print register or memory value |
| `disas [addr] [N]` | | Disassemble N instructions |
| `uart` | | Show UART output buffer |
| `uart send <val>` | | Send byte to UART RX (decimal, 0xHH, or "string") |
| `led` | | Show LED D2 and button S2 state |
| `button [press\|release\|toggle]` | `btn` | Control button S2 |
| `load <file.lgo>` | | Load a new LGO file |
| `reset` | | Reset CPU to initial state |
| `quit` | `q` | Exit debugger |

Addresses accept decimal, `0x` hex, or `0b` binary.
An empty line repeats the last command (useful for repeated stepping).

## Use Cases

### Debugging a simple program step by step

```
$ cor24-dbg tests/programs/count_down.lgo
Loaded 22 bytes from tests/programs/count_down.lgo
PC = 0x000000

(cor24) disas 0 12
=> 000000: 80           push fp
   000001: 65           mov  fp,sp
   000002: 2B 00 01 FF  la   r2,0xFF0100
   000006: 44 05        lc   r0,5
   000008: 5A           mov  r1,r0
   000009: 0A 30        add  r1,48
   00000B: 85 00        sb   r1,(r2)
   00000D: 09 FF        add  r0,-1
   00000F: C8           ceq  r0,z
   000010: 14 F4        brf  0x000008
   000012: 69           mov  sp,fp
   000013: 7C           pop  fp

(cor24) b 0x0B
Breakpoint 1 at 0x00000B

(cor24) run
Breakpoint at 0x00000B
0x00000B: sb   r1,(r2)
  r0=000005 r1=000035 r2=FF0100 fp=FEEBFD sp=FEEBFD c=0

(cor24) p r1
r1 = 0x000035 (53)          # ASCII '5'

(cor24) c
5Breakpoint at 0x00000B      # printed '5', hit breakpoint again
0x00000B: sb   r1,(r2)
  r0=000004 r1=000034 r2=FF0100 fp=FEEBFD sp=FEEBFD c=0

(cor24) delete all
All breakpoints deleted.

(cor24) run
4321
Stopped after 100000000 instructions (limit).
```

### Inspecting LED and button state

```
$ cor24-dbg tests/programs/led_blink.lgo

(cor24) led
LED D2: OFF (bit0 = 0)
Button S2: HIGH (bit0 = 1)

(cor24) step 20
  r0=... r1=... ...

(cor24) led
LED D2: ON (bit0 = 1)

(cor24) button press
Button S2: pressed (LOW)

(cor24) step 5

(cor24) p 0xFF0000
[0xFF0000] = 0x00           # button reads low

(cor24) button release
Button S2: released (HIGH)
```

### Running the sieve benchmark

```
$ cor24-dbg --entry 0x93 docs/research/asld24/sieve.lgo
Loaded 346 bytes

(cor24) run 500000000
1000 iterations
1899 primes.

Stopped after 500000000 instructions (limit).

(cor24) uart
UART output buffer (29 chars):
1000 iterations
1899 primes.
```

### Examining UART I/O registers

```
(cor24) x /4 0xFF0100
0xFF0100: 00 02 00 00  |....|
           ^  ^
           |  +-- status: bit1=CTS active, bit7=TX not busy
           +---- data register
```

### Loading assembled programs

The full pipeline from source to debug session:

```bash
# 1. Write your program
cat > mytest.s << 'EOF'
_main:
    lc   r0,42
    la   r1,-65536       ; 0xFF0000 LED address
    sb   r0,0(r1)
_halt:
    bra  _halt
EOF

# 2. Assemble
cor24-as < mytest.s | longlgo > mytest.lgo

# 3. Debug
cor24-dbg mytest.lgo
```

## Memory Map

| Region | Address Range | Description |
|--------|---------------|-------------|
| SRAM | 0x000000 - 0x0FFFFF | 1MB main memory |
| EBR | 0xFEE000 - 0xFEFFFF | 3 KB on MachXO (8 KB address range) |
| Stack | grows down from 0xFEEC00 | Initial SP |
| LED/Switch | 0xFF0000 | bit 0: LED D2 / button S2 |
| Int Enable | 0xFF0010 | bit 0: UART RX interrupt |
| UART Data | 0xFF0100 | Read: RX data, Write: TX data |
| UART Status | 0xFF0101 | bit0=RX ready, bit1=CTS, bit7=TX busy |

## Demo Scripts

Runnable demo scripts are in `scripts/`. Each builds the debugger and runs an
example program non-interactively:

| Script | What it demonstrates |
|--------|---------------------|
| `demo-cli-hello-world.sh` | UART string output, captures output into a shell variable |
| `demo-cli-count-down.sh` | Breakpoints, single-stepping, register inspection |
| `demo-cli-led-blink.sh` | LED toggling, UART output from a blink loop |
| `demo-cli-sieve.sh` | Sieve benchmark (500M instructions), UART result |

### Capturing UART output in a script

The hello-world demo shows how to extract UART output into a shell variable
for use in pipelines:

```bash
# Run the emulator and capture all output
RAW_OUTPUT=$(cor24-dbg tests/programs/hello_world.lgo <<'CMDS'
run 1000
uart
quit
CMDS
)

# Extract the UART content between the header and the next prompt
UART_OUTPUT=$(echo "$RAW_OUTPUT" | \
  awk '/UART output buffer/{found=1; next} found && /[(]cor24[)]/{found=0} found && NF{print}')

echo "$UART_OUTPUT"   # "Hello, World!"
```

## Test Programs

Source and pre-assembled `.lgo` files live in `tests/programs/`:

| Program | Description | Expected UART output |
|---------|-------------|---------------------|
| `hello_world.s` | String loop printing to UART | `Hello, World!\n` |
| `hello_uart.s` | Inline character-by-character print | `Hi\n` |
| `count_down.s` | Loop counting 5→1 with ASCII conversion | `54321` |
| `led_blink.s` | Toggle LED D2 five times, print `L` each | `LLLLL` |
| `led_on.s` | Write 1 to LED register | (LED on, no UART) |

The sieve benchmark is at `docs/research/asld24/sieve.lgo` (entry point `0x93`).

## Tips

- Use `step` then press Enter repeatedly to keep stepping (empty line = repeat)
- Use `next` to step over function calls (`jal`)
- Branch targets in disassembly show the resolved address, not the raw offset
- The `run` command accepts a cycle count: `run 1000000` for 1M instructions
- Use `_` separators for readability: `run 500_000_000`

All green. Summary of changes:

**New demo** — `scripts/demo-cli-blinky-s2.sh` (executable). Builds `cor24-emu`, runs `blinky_s2.lgo` with S2 released and with `--switch on`, dumps the LED/switch I/O lines, and points at the integration test for the toggle-during-run case.

Without this fix the demo's `--switch on` step looked broken; with it, the demo prints `LED D2: 0x00 ON` as expected. `cargo test --workspace` is green.

# COR24 emulator — I2C and SPI peripheral support

Plan for adding I2C support to the COR24 ISA emulator now, with a parallel
design sketched for SPI to add later. Targets the existing Rust emulator
at `sw-cor24-emulator.git` (the same crate that already emulates LED/switch
and UART at the addresses mapped by the COR24-TB FPGA design).

## 1. Three-layer scope

This work has three distinct deliverables, and most design choices fall
out of getting the boundary between them right:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 1: Guest applications                                     │
│   C programs + libi2c / libspi running on the COR24             │
│   (already exist in i2cspi/tmp101 and i2cspi/tmp125)            │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┘
                       │ MMIO writes/reads to GPIO-style addresses
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 2: Bus MMIO emulation (in CPU emulator core)              │
│   Models the FPGA's I2C/SPI line registers exactly. Reconstructs│
│   logical bus events from line transitions. Routes events to    │
│   whatever device(s) are currently attached.                    │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┘
                       │ Bus event API: on_start / on_byte / on_stop / ...
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 3: Pluggable virtual devices                              │
│   Implementations of an I2cSlave / SpiSlave trait for each chip │
│   we want to model: TMP101, TMP125, DS3231 RTC, BME280, an LCD, │
│   rotary encoder, EEPROMs, etc. New devices = new files.        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Layers 1 and 3 grow independently over time (more demos, more
chip models). Layer 2 is small, central, and ideally written once.

The unstated fourth concern — **demoability** — is that layer 1 examples

9	## Why this brief exists
10	
11	The web demo at `web-sw-cor24-x-assembler` is adding an I2C RTC card
12	+ demo. The web side can't ship its panel until the device
13	implementation lands in the emulator. The DS1307 is the simplest
14	popular I2C RTC — recommended in
15	[`sw-cor24-x-assembler/docs/i2c-rt2-research.txt`](../../../dwxas/github/sw-embed/sw-cor24-x-assembler/docs/i2c-rt2-research.txt)
16	— so this is the chip to add first; later RTCs (PCF8563, DS3231)
17	can grow as new device files.
18	
19	## The change
20	
21	Add a new I2C slave at
22	`sw-cor24-emulator/src/peripherals/i2c/devices/ds1307.rs` that
23	mirrors the DS1307 protocol exactly, so the same guest-side bit-bang
24	that talks to real hardware works against the emulated chip. Closest
25	existing template: `tmp101.rs` (also pointer-then-data, also a small
26	register array).
27	
28	## Register map (BCD, 8 bytes total)
29	
30	7-bit address `0x68` (write address 0xD0, read 0xD1).
31	
32	| Pointer | Field | Range | Notes |
33	|---|---|---|---|
34	| 0x00 | Seconds | 00–59 BCD | Bit 7 = CH (Clock Halt); mask out on write to keep ticking |
35	| 0x01 | Minutes | 00–59 BCD | |
36	| 0x02 | Hours   | 00–23 BCD | Bit 6 = 12/24 mode; the demo uses 24-hr, store cleanly |
37	| 0x03 | Day of Week | 1–7 BCD | |
38	| 0x04 | Date    | 01–31 BCD | |
39	| 0x05 | Month   | 01–12 BCD | |
40	| 0x06 | Year    | 00–99 BCD | |
41	| 0x07 | Control | — | RAM / SQW / OUT bits; for v1, store-verbatim is fine |
42	
43	Auto-incrementing pointer: each read/write byte advances the
44	pointer by 1 mod 8. After 0x07 it wraps to 0x00 (matches the
45	datasheet's RAM-overflow behaviour).
46	
47	## Suggested struct shape
48	
49	```rust
50	pub const DEFAULT_ADDRESS: u8 = 0x68;
51	
52	pub struct Ds1307Device {
53	    address: u8,
54	    pointer: u8,
55	    write_idx: u8,
56	    /// Eight bytes: [sec, min, hr, dow, date, month, year, ctrl].
57	    regs: [u8; 8],
58	}
59	
60	impl Ds1307Device {
61	    pub fn new(address: u8) -> Self { /* zeroed, CH bit clear */ }
62	
63	    /// Set the full clock from binary integers; the impl handles
64	    /// the BCD conversion. Used by the web UI's "set to system
65	    /// time" button.
66	    pub fn set_time(&mut self, hour: u8, min: u8, sec: u8) { ... }
67	    pub fn set_date(&mut self, year: u8, month: u8, date: u8, dow: u8) { ... }
68	
69	    /// Read back as binary integers, for the web panel snapshot.
70	    pub fn hour(&self) -> u8 { /* bcd_to_int(regs[2] & 0x3F) */ }
71	    pub fn minute(&self) -> u8 { ... }
72	    pub fn second(&self) -> u8 { ... }
73	    /* etc. */
74	
75	    /// Advance the clock by one second; cascades into minutes,
76	    /// hours, day-of-week, date, month, year as needed. The web
77	    /// run-loop can call this each emulated wall-clock second so
78	    /// the displayed time actually ticks while a demo runs.
79	    pub fn tick_second(&mut self) { ... }
80	}
81	```
82	
83	BCD helpers (per the research doc):
84	
85	```rust
86	fn int_to_bcd(n: u8) -> u8 { ((n / 10) << 4) | (n % 10) }
87	fn bcd_to_int(b: u8) -> u8 { ((b >> 4) * 10) + (b & 0x0F) }
88	```
89	
90	`I2cDevice` impl mirrors TMP101's:
91	- `on_start` resets `write_idx = 0`.
92	- `on_write_byte`: idx 0 = pointer load (mask to low 3 bits, 0..=7);
93	  idx 1.. = data byte at `regs[pointer]`, then `pointer = (pointer + 1) & 7`.
94	  On writes to register 0x00, mask CH (bit 7) so the clock keeps
95	  running regardless of what the master tries.
96	- `on_read_byte`: return `regs[pointer]`, then advance pointer.
97	- ACK every byte (DS1307 ACKs liberally).

# Brief: add `Ds1307Device` to `sw-cor24-emulator`

**Owner:** dcemu
**Branch:** `pr/i2c-ds1307-device` (in dcemu's primary clone)
**Repo:** `sw-cor24-emulator`
**Drafted by:** dwxas
**Date drafted:** 2026-05-16

## Why this brief exists

The web demo at `web-sw-cor24-x-assembler` is adding an I2C RTC card
+ demo. The web side can't ship its panel until the device
implementation lands in the emulator. The DS1307 is the simplest
popular I2C RTC — recommended in
[`sw-cor24-x-assembler/docs/i2c-rt2-research.txt`](../../../dwxas/github/sw-embed/sw-cor24-x-assembler/docs/i2c-rt2-research.txt)
— so this is the chip to add first; later RTCs (PCF8563, DS3231)
can grow as new device files.

## The change

Add a new I2C slave at
`sw-cor24-emulator/src/peripherals/i2c/devices/ds1307.rs` that
mirrors the DS1307 protocol exactly, so the same guest-side bit-bang
that talks to real hardware works against the emulated chip. Closest
existing template: `tmp101.rs` (also pointer-then-data, also a small
register array).

## Register map (BCD, 8 bytes total)

7-bit address `0x68` (write address 0xD0, read 0xD1).

| Pointer | Field | Range | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0x00 | Seconds | 00–59 BCD | Bit 7 = CH (Clock Halt); mask out on write to keep ticking |
| 0x01 | Minutes | 00–59 BCD | |
| 0x02 | Hours   | 00–23 BCD | Bit 6 = 12/24 mode; the demo uses 24-hr, store cleanly |
| 0x03 | Day of Week | 1–7 BCD | |
| 0x04 | Date    | 01–31 BCD | |
| 0x05 | Month   | 01–12 BCD | |
| 0x06 | Year    | 00–99 BCD | |
| 0x07 | Control | — | RAM / SQW / OUT bits; for v1, store-verbatim is fine |

Auto-incrementing pointer: each read/write byte advances the
pointer by 1 mod 8. After 0x07 it wraps to 0x00 (matches the
datasheet's RAM-overflow behaviour).

## Suggested struct shape

```rust
pub const DEFAULT_ADDRESS: u8 = 0x68;

pub struct Ds1307Device {
    address: u8,
    pointer: u8,
    write_idx: u8,
    /// Eight bytes: [sec, min, hr, dow, date, month, year, ctrl].
    regs: [u8; 8],
}

impl Ds1307Device {
    pub fn new(address: u8) -> Self { /* zeroed, CH bit clear */ }

    /// Set the full clock from binary integers; the impl handles
    /// the BCD conversion. Used by the web UI's "set to system
    /// time" button.
    pub fn set_time(&mut self, hour: u8, min: u8, sec: u8) { ... }
    pub fn set_date(&mut self, year: u8, month: u8, date: u8, dow: u8) { ... }

    /// Read back as binary integers, for the web panel snapshot.
    pub fn hour(&self) -> u8 { /* bcd_to_int(regs[2] & 0x3F) */ }
    pub fn minute(&self) -> u8 { ... }
    pub fn second(&self) -> u8 { ... }
    /* etc. */

    /// Advance the clock by one second; cascades into minutes,
    /// hours, day-of-week, date, month, year as needed. The web
    /// run-loop can call this each emulated wall-clock second so
    /// the displayed time actually ticks while a demo runs.
    pub fn tick_second(&mut self) { ... }
}
```

BCD helpers (per the research doc):

```rust
fn int_to_bcd(n: u8) -> u8 { ((n / 10) << 4) | (n % 10) }
fn bcd_to_int(b: u8) -> u8 { ((b >> 4) * 10) + (b & 0x0F) }
```

`I2cDevice` impl mirrors TMP101's:
- `on_start` resets `write_idx = 0`.
- `on_write_byte`: idx 0 = pointer load (mask to low 3 bits, 0..=7);
  idx 1.. = data byte at `regs[pointer]`, then `pointer = (pointer + 1) & 7`.
  On writes to register 0x00, mask CH (bit 7) so the clock keeps
  running regardless of what the master tries.
- `on_read_byte`: return `regs[pointer]`, then advance pointer.
- ACK every byte (DS1307 ACKs liberally).

## Tests

Co-locate with the device, like `tmp101.rs`'s tests:
- BCD round-trip helpers
- Read at pointer 0x00 returns 7 bytes in order, pointer wraps after 0x07
- Write with pointer-load then 7 data bytes lands them in `regs`
- CH bit is masked out on write
- `tick_second()` cascades correctly across minute / hour / day
  boundaries (including end-of-month — 31 → next month, 30 → next
  on April etc.; leap-year handling is OK to defer to a follow-up)

## Acceptance

- `src/peripherals/i2c/devices/ds1307.rs` lands.
- Re-exported from `src/peripherals/i2c/devices/mod.rs` and the
  parent `src/peripherals/i2c/mod.rs` matches the TMP101 / Add1
  re-export shape.
- `cargo test` green (per-device unit tests + integration if any).
- `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` clean.

## Sibling-clone hygiene for dwxas

Once dcemu's `pr/i2c-ds1307-device` relays into
`sw-cor24-emulator/origin/dev`, dwxas refreshes their sibling clone
and consumes the device in the web-side step 012 (panel + demo).

## Reference reading

- Research/spec: [`sw-cor24-x-assembler/docs/i2c-rt2-research.txt`](../../../dwxas/github/sw-embed/sw-cor24-x-assembler/docs/i2c-rt2-research.txt)
- Closest template: `sw-cor24-emulator/src/peripherals/i2c/devices/tmp101.rs`
- Test slave precedent: `sw-cor24-emulator/src/peripherals/i2c/devices/add1.rs`

i2c-rt2-research.txt
Conversation with Gemini
which I2C RTC is the simplest? I want to emulate it in software, so fewer registers/commands and simpler is preferred to full-function or advanced. what RTCs are the most popular and rank then from easiest to emulate to hardest. Describe the registers/commands for the simplest one with example I2C calls to get the time (and set the time, though the simulated device will be initialized to the system time)

For a software emulation project, the DS1307 is hands-down the absolute simplest and most straightforward standard I2C Real-Time Clock to implement.

Unlike newer or more fully-featured RTCs, the DS1307 lacks complex features like built-in temperature sensors, integrated alarms, customizable countdown timers, or multi-byte status/control structures. Its core timekeeping relies entirely on an array of standard Binary Coded Decimal (BCD) values mapped linearly across a sequence of registers.  

Popular I2C RTCs Ranked (Easiest to Hardest to Emulate)
1. DS1307 (Easiest)
Why it's easy: It features a linear map of 7 basic time registers (address 0x00 to 0x06). It lacks alarms or elaborate internal state flags. You only need to emulate simple byte increments and basic BCD conversion logic.  

2. PCF8563
Why it's slightly harder: While highly popular, its time registers start at address 0x02 instead of 0x00. The first two registers (0x00 and 0x01) are dedicated to control and status flags. It also incorporates alarms, timers, and an explicit century-overflow bit which adds extra register masking logic to your code.

3. DS3231 (Hardest of the popular options)
Why it's hardest: The DS3231 is incredibly popular because it is temperature-compensated and highly accurate. However, this means your emulation must handle temperature registers, aging offset registers, control/status bit arrays, multiple configurable alarm registers, and push-button reset handling.  

DS1307 Register Map
The DS1307 uses a standard 7-bit I2C slave address of 0x68.  

Data is strictly handled in Binary Coded Decimal (BCD) format. For example, a value of 45 seconds is represented as 0x45 (where the high nibble 4 represents the tens place, and the low nibble 5 represents the ones place).  

Register Address	Bit 7 (MSB)	Bit 6	Bit 5	Bit 4	Bit 3	Bit 2	Bit 1	Bit 0 (LSB)	Range (BCD)
0x00	CH (Clock Halt)	-	-	-	-	-	-	-	Seconds (00–59)
0x01	-	-	-	-	-	-	-	-	Minutes (00–59)
0x02	0	12/24	AM/PM	10 Hr	-	-	-	-	Hours (01–12 / 00–23)
0x03	0	0	0	0	0	-	-	-	Day of Week (01–07)
0x04	0	0	-	-	-	-	-	-	Date of Month (01–31)
0x05	0	0	0	-	-	-	-	-	Month (01–12)
0x06	-	-	-	-	-	-	-	-	Year (00–99)
⚠️ Emulation Tip: Bit 7 of register 0x00 is the CH (Clock Halt) bit. If it is set to 1, the clock stops ticking. To keep things running smoothly, your emulator can simply ignore this bit or force register 0x00 to mask it out. Bit 6 of register 0x02 switches between 12-hour or 24-hour mode. If you want the absolute simplest emulation logic, expect the master to use standard 24-hour mode (Bit 6 = 0).  
+1

Example I2C Transactions
The DS1307 uses an auto-incrementing address pointer. When you talk to it, the first byte after the I2C address specifies the starting register. Every byte read or written afterward automatically increments that pointer by 1.

1. Reading the Time (Master Request)
To get the current time, the host master performs a combined transaction: it writes the starting register pointer (0x00), executes an I2C Restart, and then reads 7 sequential bytes.

Plaintext
[START] -> Write Address (0xD0) -> Register Pointer (0x00) -> [RESTART] -> Read Address (0xD1)
                                                                   |
    [0x30] (30 Seconds) <------------------------------------------+ (Master ACKs)
    [0x45] (45 Minutes) <------------------------------------------+ (Master ACKs)
    [0x14] (14 Hours / 2:00 PM) <----------------------------------+ (Master ACKs)
    [0x03] (Tuesday / Day 3) <-------------------------------------+ (Master ACKs)
    [0x16] (16th Day of Month) <-----------------------------------+ (Master ACKs)
    [0x05] (May / Month 5) <---------------------------------------+ (Master ACKs)
    [0x26] (Year 2026) <-------------------------------------------+ [STOP] (Master NACKs)
(Note: I2C write address 0xD0 and read address 0xD1 represent the 7-bit address 0x68 shifted left by 1 bit with the R/W bit added).

2. Setting the Time (Master Write)
To overwrite or initialize the clock, the master sends the starting register point followed immediately by the raw BCD configuration bytes.

Plaintext
[START] -> Write Address (0xD0) 
               |
               +--> Register Pointer (0x00)
               +--> Data 0x00 (00 Seconds, clear CH bit)
               +--> Data 0x15 (15 Minutes)
               +--> Data 0x09 (09 Hours)
               +--> Data 0x03 (Day 3)
               +--> Data 0x16 (16th Day)
               +--> Data 0x05 (Month 5)
               +--> Data 0x26 (Year 2026) -> [STOP]
Essential Emulation Math
When your software emulator intercepts a read request, it translates your system's raw integers into BCD formats. You can map this transformation with these formulas:

Integer to BCD=((Value/10)≪4)∣(Value%10)
BCD to Integer=((Value≫4)×10)+(Value & 0x0F)

which I2C RTC is the simplest? I want to emulate it in software, so fewer registers/commands and simpler is preferred to full-function or advanced. what RTCs are the most popular and rank then from easiest to emulate to hardest. Describe the registers/commands for the simplest one with example I2C calls to get the time (and set the time, though the simulated device will be initialized to the system time)

For a software emulation project, the DS1307 is hands-down the absolute simplest and most straightforward standard I2C Real-Time Clock to implement.

Unlike newer or more fully-featured RTCs, the DS1307 lacks complex features like built-in temperature sensors, integrated alarms, customizable countdown timers, or multi-byte status/control structures. Its core timekeeping relies entirely on an array of standard Binary Coded Decimal (BCD) values mapped linearly across a sequence of registers.  

Popular I2C RTCs Ranked (Easiest to Hardest to Emulate)
1. DS1307 (Easiest)
Why it's easy: It features a linear map of 7 basic time registers (address 0x00 to 0x06). It lacks alarms or elaborate internal state flags. You only need to emulate simple byte increments and basic BCD conversion logic.  

2. PCF8563
Why it's slightly harder: While highly popular, its time registers start at address 0x02 instead of 0x00. The first two registers (0x00 and 0x01) are dedicated to control and status flags. It also incorporates alarms, timers, and an explicit century-overflow bit which adds extra register masking logic to your code.

3. DS3231 (Hardest of the popular options)
Why it's hardest: The DS3231 is incredibly popular because it is temperature-compensated and highly accurate. However, this means your emulation must handle temperature registers, aging offset registers, control/status bit arrays, multiple configurable alarm registers, and push-button reset handling.  

DS1307 Register Map
The DS1307 uses a standard 7-bit I2C slave address of 0x68.  

Data is strictly handled in Binary Coded Decimal (BCD) format. For example, a value of 45 seconds is represented as 0x45 (where the high nibble 4 represents the tens place, and the low nibble 5 represents the ones place).

0x00	CH (Clock Halt)	-	-	-	-	-	-	-	Seconds (00–59)
0x01	-	-	-	-	-	-	-	-	Minutes (00–59)
0x02	0	12/24	AM/PM	10 Hr	-	-	-	-	Hours (01–12 / 00–23)
0x03	0	0	0	0	0	-	-	-	Day of Week (01–07)
0x04	0	0	-	-	-	-	-	-	Date of Month (01–31)
0x05	0	0	0	-	-	-	-	-	Month (01–12)
0x06	-	-	-	-	-	-	-	-	Year (00–99)
⚠️ Emulation Tip: Bit 7 of register 0x00 is the CH (Clock Halt) bit. If it is set to 1, the clock stops ticking. To keep things running smoothly, your emulator can simply ignore this bit or force register 0x00 to mask it out. Bit 6 of register 0x02 switches between 12-hour or 24-hour mode. 1	# MakerLisp COR24 CLI Emulator Guide
2	
3	The `cor24-dbg` debugger lets you load, run, step through, and inspect
4	[MakerLisp](https://makerlisp.com) COR24 programs assembled with the
5	reference `as24` toolchain.
6	
7	## Quick Start
8	
9	### 1. Assemble a program
10	
11	```bash
12	# Assemble and link into LGO format
13	cor24-as < tests/programs/hello_uart.s | longlgo > hello_uart.lgo
14	
15	# View the listing to see addresses and opcodes
16	cor24-as -l < tests/programs/hello_uart.s
17	```
18	
19	### 2. Run in the debugger
20	
21	```bash
22	cor24-dbg hello_uart.lgo
23	```
24	
25	If the program's entry point is not at address 0 (e.g. sieve.lgo has
26	`_main` at 0x93):
27	
28	```bash
29	cor24-dbg --entry 0x93 docs/research/asld24/sieve.lgo
30	```
31	
32	### 3. Debug
33	
34	```
35	(cor24) run                  # run until halt/breakpoint/limit
36	(cor24) step                 # single step one instruction
37	(cor24) step 10              # step 10 instructions
38	(cor24) info                 # show all registers
39	(cor24) disas                # disassemble at PC
40	(cor24) x /16 0xFF0100       # examine 16 bytes at UART address
41	```
42	
43	## Command Reference
44	
45	| Command | Short | Description |
46	|---------|-------|-------------|
47	| `run [N]` | `r` | Run N instructions (default 100M) |
48	| `step [N]` | `s` | Single step N instructions |
49	| `next` | `n` | Step over (skip into jal calls) |
50	| `continue` | `c` | Continue from breakpoint |
51	| `break <addr>` | `b` | Set breakpoint at address |
52	| `delete <N\|all>` | `d` | Delete breakpoint(s) |
53	| `info [r\|b]` | `i` | Show registers or breakpoints |
54	| `examine [/N] <addr>` | `x` | Examine N bytes at address |
55	| `print <reg\|addr>` | `p` | Print register or memory value |
56	| `disas [addr] [N]` | | Disassemble N instructions |
57	| `uart` | | Show UART output buffer |
58	| `uart send <val>` | | Send byte to UART RX (decimal, 0xHH, or "string") |
59	| `led` | | Show LED D2 and button S2 state |
60	| `button [press\|release\|toggle]` | `btn` | Control button S2 |
61	| `load <file.lgo>` | | Load a new LGO file |
62	| `reset` | | Reset CPU to initial state |
63	| `quit` | `q` | Exit debugger |
64	
65	Addresses accept decimal, `0x` hex, or `0b` binary.
66	An empty line repeats the last command (useful for repeated stepping).
67	
68	## Use Cases
69	
70	### Debugging a simple program step by step
71	
72	```
73	$ cor24-dbg tests/programs/count_down.lgo
74	Loaded 22 bytes from tests/programs/count_down.lgo
75	PC = 0x000000
76	
77	(cor24) disas 0 12
78	=> 000000: 80           push fp
79	   000001: 65           mov  fp,sp
80	   000002: 2B 00 01 FF  la   r2,0xFF0100
81	   000006: 44 05        lc   r0,5
82	   000008: 5A           mov  r1,r0
83	   000009: 0A 30        add  r1,48
84	   00000B: 85 00        sb   r1,(r2)
85	   00000D: 09 FF        add  r0,-1
86	   00000F: C8           ceq  r0,z
87	   000010: 14 F4        brf  0x000008
88	   000012: 69           mov  sp,fp
89	   000013: 7C           pop  fp
90	
91	(cor24) b 0x0B
92	Breakpoint 1 at 0x00000B
93	
94	(cor24) run
95	Breakpoint at 0x00000B
96	0x00000B: sb   r1,(r2)
97	  r0=000005 r1=000035 r2=FF0100 fp=FEEBFD sp=FEEBFD c=0
98	
99	(cor24) p r1
100	r1 = 0x000035 (53)          # ASCII '5'
101	
102	(cor24) c
103	5Breakpoint at 0x00000B      # printed '5', hit breakpoint again
104	0x00000B: sb   r1,(r2)
105	  r0=000004 r1=000034 r2=FF0100 fp=FEEBFD sp=FEEBFD c=0
106	
107	(cor24) delete all
108	All breakpoints deleted.
109	
110	(cor24) run
111	4321
112	Stopped after 100000000 instructions (limit).
113	```
114	
115	### Inspecting LED and button state
116	
117	```
118	$ cor24-dbg tests/programs/led_blink.lgo
119	
120	(cor24) led
121	LED D2: OFF (bit0 = 0)
122	Button S2: HIGH (bit0 = 1)
123	
124	(cor24) step 20
125	  r0=... r1=... ...
126	
127	(cor24) led
128	LED D2: ON (bit0 = 1)
129	
130	(cor24) button press
131	Button S2: pressed (LOW)
132	
133	(cor24) step 5
134	
135	(cor24) p 0xFF0000
136	[0xFF0000] = 0x00           # button reads low
137	
138	(cor24) button release
139	Button S2: released (HIGH)
140	```
141	
142	### Running the sieve benchmark
143	
144	```
145	$ cor24-dbg --entry 0x93 docs/research/asld24/sieve.lgo
146	Loaded 346 bytes
147	
148	(cor24) run 500000000
149	1000 iterations
150	1899 primes.
151	
152	Stopped after 500000000 instructions (limit).
153	
154	(cor24) uart
155	UART output buffer (29 chars):
156	1000 iterations
157	1899 primes.
158	```
159	
160	### Examining UART I/O registers
161	
162	```
163	(cor24) x /4 0xFF0100
164	0xFF0100: 00 02 00 00  |....|
165	           ^  ^
166	           |  +-- status: bit1=CTS active, bit7=TX not busy
167	           +---- data register
168	```
169	
170	### Loading assembled programs
171	
172	The full pipeline from source to debug session:
173	
174	```bash
175	# 1. Write your program
176	cat > mytest.s << 'EOF'
177	_main:
178	    lc   r0,42
179	    la   r1,-65536       ; 0xFF0000 LED address
180	    sb   r0,0(r1)
181	_halt:
182	    bra  _halt
183	EOF
184	
185	# 2. Assemble
186	cor24-as < mytest.s | longlgo > mytest.lgo
187	
188	# 3. Debug
189	cor24-dbg mytest.lgo
190	```
191	
192	## Memory Map
193	
194	| Region | Address Range | Description |
195	|--------|---------------|-------------|
196	| SRAM | 0x000000 - 0x0FFFFF | 1MB main memory |
197	| EBR | 0xFEE000 - 0xFEFFFF | 3 KB on MachXO (8 KB address range) |
198	| Stack | grows down from 0xFEEC00 | Initial SP |
199	| LED/Switch | 0xFF0000 | bit 0: LED D2 / button S2 |
200	| Int Enable | 0xFF0010 | bit 0: UART RX interrupt |
201	| UART Data | 0xFF0100 | Read: RX data, Write: TX data |
202	| UART Status | 0xFF0101 | bit0=RX ready, bit1=CTS, bit7=TX busy |
203	
204	## Demo Scripts
205	
206	Runnable demo scripts are in `scripts/`. Each builds the debugger and runs an
207	example program non-interactively:
208	
209	| Script | What it demonstrates |
210	|--------|---------------------|
211	| `demo-cli-hello-world.sh` | UART string output, captures output into a shell variable |
212	| `demo-cli-count-down.sh` | Breakpoints, single-stepping, register inspection |
213	| `demo-cli-led-blink.sh` | LED toggling, UART output from a blink loop |
214	| `demo-cli-sieve.sh` | Sieve benchmark (500M instructions), UART result |
215	
216	### Capturing UART output in a script
217	
218	The hello-world demo shows how to extract UART output into a shell variable
219	for use in pipelines:
220	
221	```bash
222	# Run the emulator and capture all output
223	RAW_OUTPUT=$(cor24-dbg tests/programs/hello_world.lgo <<'CMDS'
224	run 1000
225	uart
226	quit
227	CMDS
228	)
229	
230	# Extract the UART content between the header and the next prompt
231	UART_OUTPUT=$(echo "$RAW_OUTPUT" | \
232	  awk '/UART output buffer/{found=1; next} found && /[(]cor24[)]/{found=0} found && NF{print}')
233	
234	echo "$UART_OUTPUT"   # "Hello, World!"
235	```
236	
237	## Test Programs
238	
239	Source and pre-assembled `.lgo` files live in `tests/programs/`:
240	
241	| Program | Description | Expected UART output |
242	|---------|-------------|---------------------|
243	| `hello_world.s` | String loop printing to UART | `Hello, World!\n` |
244	| `hello_uart.s` | Inline character-by-character print | `Hi\n` |
245	| `count_down.s` | Loop counting 5→1 with ASCII conversion | `54321` |
246	| `led_blink.s` | Toggle LED D2 five times, print `L` each | `LLLLL` |
247	| `led_on.s` | Write 1 to LED register | (LED on, no UART) |
248	
249	The sieve benchmark is at `docs/research/asld24/sieve.lgo` (entry point `0x93`).
250	
251	## Tips
252	
253	- Use `step` then press Enter repeatedly to keep stepping (empty line = repeat)
254	- Use `next` to step over function calls (`jal`)
255	- Branch targets in disassembly show the resolved address, not the raw offset
256	- The `run` command accepts a cycle count: `run 1000000` for 1M instructions
257	- Use `_` separators for readability: `run 500_000_000`

feat(i2c): Ds1307Device — DS1307 RTC slave at 0x68

Adds the simplest popular I2C RTC as a new device file, modeled on
tmp101.rs (pointer-then-data with an 8-byte register array).

- src/peripherals/i2c/devices/ds1307.rs:
  - 8 BCD registers behind an auto-incrementing pointer that wraps
    after 0x07 (matches the datasheet's RAM-overflow behaviour).
  - Bit 7 (CH) on register 0x00 is masked on writes so the emulated
    clock keeps ticking regardless of what the master sends.
  - set_time / set_date take binary integers and do the BCD encoding;
    the per-field getters mask the format bits and BCD-decode back.
  - tick_second() cascades into minutes/hours/day-of-week/date/month/
    year with month-length awareness. Leap-year handling is deferred
    per the brief — February is fixed at 28 days.
  - Ds1307HandleExt provides the I2cHandle ergonomic shortcuts
    (set_time, hour(), tick_second(), ...).
  - 17 unit tests covering BCD round-trip, sequential 7-byte reads,
    pointer wrap and masking, CH-bit masking, and cascade boundaries
    at minute / hour / day / 30-day month / 31-day month / February /
    year / year-99 wrap.

  if git rev-parse --verify --quiet origin/dev >/dev/null \
     && git merge-base --is-ancestor "$pr" origin/dev 2>/dev/null; then

    echo "reaped:  $pr"
    reaped=$((reaped+1))
  else
    echo "pending: $pr (not yet in origin/dev)"
    pending=$((pending+1))
  fi
done < <(git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)' refs/heads/pr refs/heads/pr/\*)

1	//! `ds1307` — Maxim/Dallas DS1307 real-time clock (I2C).
2	//!
3	//! Eight BCD registers behind an auto-incrementing pointer, exactly as
4	//! the datasheet describes. The web UI's RTC panel reads/writes them
5	//! through the same bit-bang path a real master would use, so this
6	//! device mirrors the chip's protocol rather than offering a friendly
7	//! out-of-band interface.
8	//!
9	//! Pointer mapping (`pointer & 0x07`):
10	//!   - `0x00` — Seconds (00–59 BCD). Bit 7 = CH (Clock Halt) — masked
11	//!     out on writes so the emulated clock keeps ticking regardless.
12	//!   - `0x01` — Minutes (00–59 BCD).
13	//!   - `0x02` — Hours (00–23 BCD). Bit 6 = 12/24 mode; this device
14	//!     stores 24-hour format.
15	//!   - `0x03` — Day of Week (1–7 BCD).
16	//!   - `0x04` — Date (01–31 BCD).
17	//!   - `0x05` — Month (01–12 BCD).
18	//!   - `0x06` — Year (00–99 BCD).
19	//!   - `0x07` — Control. Stored verbatim; the SQW/RAM/OUT bits don't
20	//!     affect timekeeping in this emulation.
21	
22	use crate::peripherals::i2c::device::{Ack, I2cDevice};
23	
24	/// Default 7-bit address for the DS1307.

28	const REG_MINUTES: usize = 1;

All green. Now the analysis you asked for — pausing before I commit, since your note reframes what the API surface should look like.

## Analysis: battery-backed DS1307

### What the current device does today (after my WIP)

| Concern | Current state |
|---|---|
| Power-on default | All-zero registers: 00:00:00 on 00/00/00, CH bit clear. ✅ matches "starts at 0:00:00 when powered on" |
| Continuous ticking | Master (or web run-loop) calls `tick_second()` per emulated wall-clock second. Chip doesn't auto-tick |
| Seed from host clock | `set_to_system_time()` reads `SystemTime::now()`. Opt-in only |
| Seed from arbitrary epoch | `set_from_unix_seconds(secs)` |
| CLI seed flag | `?init=now` (opt-in; default is still zero) |

The default already matches "zero on power-up." Nothing to revert.

### Where "battery-backed" should live

Real DS1307 hardware: its 32 kHz crystal keeps ticking on the Vbat coin cell. The chip itself doesn't know about "wall clock" or "how long was I unplugged" — it just has an oscillator that the battery powers.

So a faithful emulation of battery-backed RTC is just: **the chip's registers persist across sessions, and time advances by the wall-clock delta between save and restore.**

That math is fundamentally a **consumer-side persistence concern**, not a chip-emulation concern. Two reasons:

1. **Determinism.** If the device queried `SystemTime::now()` on its own to advance state, every unit test would be time-sensitive. The current `tick_second()` design is correct: explicit external drive, deterministic state.
2. **Faithful modeling.** A real DS1307 doesn't know what wall-clock time it is — it only knows what was last written and how many oscillator ticks have happened since. The "battery saves state across power cycles" abstraction is implemented by physics, not by silicon logic. The emulator equivalent is: the consumer stores state to localStorage/disk and restores it.

### Recommended approach

**Keep the device pure. Put the persistence math in the web UI.** Pattern:

```js
// On user "Set clock" / page unload:
const rtcEpoch = computeRtcUnixFromUI();   // whatever user picked
const hostNow  = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
localStorage.setItem('ds1307', JSON.stringify({rtc: rtcEpoch, host: hostNow}));
handle.set_from_unix_seconds(rtcEpoch);

// On page load:
const saved = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('ds1307') || 'null');
if (saved) {
    const elapsed = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - saved.host;
    handle.set_from_unix_seconds(saved.rtc + elapsed);
}
// else: leave at default 0:00:00 (fresh chip, no battery / battery dead)
```

That's the whole "battery backup" — three lines on each side. The emulator never grows a wall-clock dependency.

### Changes I'd make to my WIP before committing

1. **Rename `?init=now` → `?epoch=now`** so the keyword reads as "seed the epoch register" instead of "this is the default init." Default is still zero; the param is opt-in.
2. **Add `?epoch=<unix_seconds>`** alongside `now`, so saga tests and the web UI's projected-time path can pass an explicit timestamp without going through host clock.
3. **Drop `set_to_system_time` from the public API** — leave only `set_from_unix_seconds`. The CLI registry can call `SystemTime::now()` itself when parsing `?epoch=now`. Rationale: `set_to_system_time` couples a chip method to host time, but it's only ever a one-line convenience over `set_from_unix_seconds(SystemTime::now()...)`. Removing it keeps the device fully time-agnostic; the host-clock leak is contained to the CLI parser.
4. **Add a doc block** in `ds1307.rs` describing the battery-backed pattern (consumer responsibility, sample JS snippet).

### What I'd NOT do

- ❌ Make the device track wall-clock internally — breaks determinism, doesn't match real silicon.
- ❌ Default to `now` — you explicitly said default should be zero, and that aligns with how a fresh chip with no battery actually behaves.
- ❌ Add a separate "battery present?" flag — it's a fiction; what matters is whether the consumer restored state from somewhere.

Want me to proceed with the four changes above, or do you want to push back on any part of the analysis before I commit?

The brief said cold-start hardware ought to default to all-zero

concern (the web UI saves (rtc_epoch, host_epoch) to local storage
and projects forward across sessions). Add the single emulator-side
hook that supports both:

  brief).

- Registry param --i2c-device ds1307@<addr>?epoch=<now|seconds>:
  `epoch=now` lets the CLI parser pull the host clock (the host-time
  dependency is contained at the consumer boundary, not in the chip);
  `epoch=<unix>` lets a test or the web UI pass an explicit timestamp.

- Power-on default is zero (cold-start hardware behaviour).
- Battery backup lives in the consumer's persistence layer, not in

- set_to_system_time() was added speculatively and then dropped —

2026-05-16 anchor, the 2024-02-29 leap day, 2024-03-01 post-leap,
and the 2100 century-non-leap edge), set_from_unix_seconds round

**Owner:** dcemu
**Branch:** `pr/ds1307-initial-time-and-system-preset`
**Repo:** `sw-cor24-x-assembler`'s emulator path-dep — `sw-cor24-emulator`
**Drafted by:** dcxas (2026-05-16)

## Why this brief exists

dcxas just shipped two RTC demos in the assembler repo:
`i2c_ds1307_read.s` (passive observer, prints `HH:MM:SS\n`) and
`i2c_ds1307_set.s` (UART-driven setter that writes the registers
via i2c then reads them back). Both work end-to-end against
`cor24-emu --i2c-device ds1307@0x68` — but **the CLI spec accepts
no params**, so out-of-the-box the read demo prints `00:00:00`
forever. The only way to get a non-zero starting time today is
the in-Rust `Ds1307HandleExt::set_*` API (which the web panel
will use, but is unavailable to CLI users).

This brief proposes the missing CLI surface so:

- dcxas's read demo can show meaningful output from a one-liner
  without the web panel (`--i2c-device 'ds1307@0x68?preset=system'`
  shows the host clock).
- dwxas's `web-sw-cor24-x-assembler` battery-backed RTC demo
  (currently in design — see "Battery story" below) has a clean
  emulator-side hook to pass an effective initial time without
  routing through `handle.set_time`.
- The "no battery" vs "with battery" web toggle becomes a one-arg
  CLI-side difference rather than two separate Rust code paths.

## What changes

Add three things to `sw-cor24-emulator`:

1. **`Ds1307Device::with_initial_registers(...)`** — a public
   constructor that takes the 8 BCD register values (S/M/H/DoW/
   Date/Month/Year/Control) and pre-loads them. Defaults match
   `new()` (all-zero, control = 0). Use it in `new()` itself for
   the existing "all-zero" path, so there's one source of truth.
2. **Registry parser support for `ds1307@<addr>?<params>`** — in
   `src/peripherals/i2c/registry.rs::build_i2c_device`'s `"ds1307"`
   arm, accept these param keys (all optional):

   | Key      | Value         | Behavior                                  |
   |----------|---------------|-------------------------------------------|
   | `hour`   | 0-23 decimal  | Sets the Hours register (BCD-encoded; 24-hour). Conflicts with `preset`. |
   | `minute` | 0-59 decimal  | Sets Minutes. Conflicts with `preset`.     |
   | `second` | 0-59 decimal  | Sets Seconds. Conflicts with `preset`.     |
   | `date`   | 1-31 decimal  | Sets Date register. Conflicts with `preset`. |
   | `month`  | 1-12 decimal  | Sets Month. Conflicts with `preset`.       |
   | `year`   | 0-99 decimal  | Sets Year register (2-digit). Conflicts with `preset`. |
   | `dow`    | 1-7 decimal   | Sets DayOfWeek register. Conflicts with `preset`. |
   | `preset` | `system`      | Reads host clock at attach time and sets all 7 time registers from it. Conflicts with any of the above keys. |

   Reject unknown keys (current pattern). Reject out-of-range
   values with a clear error message naming both the key and the
   value (`"ds1307 'hour' out of range: 24 (valid: 0-23)"`).
   Reject `preset` with `?hour=` etc. set
   (`"ds1307 'preset' and explicit register values are mutually exclusive"`).

3. **Help text update** in the CLI:

   ```
   --i2c-device <spec>    Attach an I2C device (repeatable). Specs:
                            add1@<addr>[?wrap=<n>]                universal +1 test slave
                            tmp101@<addr>[?temp=<f>][?config=<n>] TI temp sensor
                            ds1307@<addr>[?hour=<n>][?minute=<n>]
                                  [?second=<n>][?date=<n>][?month=<n>]
                                  [?year=<n>][?dow=<n>]
                                  [?preset=system]                Dallas/Maxim RTC
   ```

That's the entire surface change. The existing
`Ds1307HandleExt::set_time / set_date / tick_second / ...` runtime
API stays as-is (it's what the web panel's slider will use for
mid-session updates).

## Tests

Add to `src/peripherals/i2c/registry.rs` test module:

- `build_ds1307_with_time_params` — `ds1307@0x68?hour=12&minute=34&second=56`
  → device address 0x68, register 0x00 = 0x56 (BCD), 0x01 = 0x34,
  0x02 = 0x12.
- `build_ds1307_with_full_date` — all 7 keys set; assert each
  register encodes correctly.
- `build_ds1307_preset_system` — `ds1307@0x68?preset=system`
  reads `std::time::SystemTime::now()` (or `chrono::Local::now()`),
  asserts the registers fall within a small window of "now" at
  test-run time (allow a few seconds of slack for test scheduling).

- `build_ds1307_out_of_range_rejected` — `?hour=24`, `?minute=60`,
  `?dow=0`, `?year=100` all rejected with named errors.

  `?temp=25.0` test passes unchanged (regression).

ds1307 end-to-end tests live: assemble the existing
`examples/i2c/tmp101/tmp101.lgo`-style fixture against
`ds1307@0x68?hour=12&minute=34&second=56`, run it through the
emulator, observe that an i2c-read of register 0x02 returns 0x12.

- **No persistence in the emulator.** Battery-backed survival
  across runs is purely a web/UI concern — see "Battery story"
  below. The emulator stays stateless across CLI invocations;
  each `--i2c-device ds1307@...` call constructs a fresh device.
- **No 12-hour mode** on the Hours register. The device already
  stores 24-hour values per its doc; `?hour=` takes 0-23
  decimal and BCD-encodes it. Bit 6 (12/24 mode flag) stays 0.
- **No SQW/OUT control bit support.** Register 0x07 stays
  default-zero. Future brief if anyone needs the squarewave
  output simulated.
- **No `?control=<n>` param.** Skip until something actually
  reads register 0x07 meaningfully.
- **No `Ds1307Device::with_system_clock()` Rust API.** Use the
  registry path (`?preset=system`) for that. Library users who
  want it can call `with_initial_registers(...)` with a chrono-
  computed argument.

## Battery story (context for the param design — not work for this brief)

The web side will offer two toggles for the RTC live demo:

- **"No battery"** — emulator gets `ds1307@0x68` with no params;
  registers boot at 0:00:00. Each page reload starts fresh.
- **"With battery"** — emulator gets `ds1307@0x68?hour=X&minute=Y&second=Z`
  where X/Y/Z come from web localStorage:

  ```javascript
  // localStorage key: "ds1307.battery"
  // value: { set_value: { h, m, s, ... }, set_at_ms: <Date.now() at set> }
  const persisted = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("ds1307.battery"));
  const elapsed_s = (Date.now() - persisted.set_at_ms) / 1000;
  const effective_total_s = (persisted.set_value.h*3600 + persisted.set_value.m*60
                             + persisted.set_value.s) + elapsed_s;

persistence machinery** — the emulator just sees a constructed
device with the right initial values. dcemu does not need to
think about localStorage, chrono in the web, or page-reload
lifecycle. dwxas owns all of that.

update localStorage synchronously with the i2c-write transaction

That's a web-side concern, not an emulator concern.

pattern already in use (`tmp101@0x4A?temp=25.0` doesn't pretend

content.text: Committed and renamed to `pr/i2c-ds1307-system-time`. Reading the new brief for refinement.

Read the brief. It significantly reshapes the API surface I just shipped (`?epoch=<now|seconds>` → per-field `?hour/?minute/.../?preset=system`, plus a `with_initial_registers` constructor as single source of truth). Let me confirm my reading before diving in:

**Brief's design vs. my just-shipped `5a92afe`:**

| | Mine (5a92afe) | Brief proposes |
|---|---|---|
| CLI keyword for host clock | `?epoch=now` | `?preset=system` |
| Per-field setting | ❌ not supported | ✅ `?hour=12&minute=34&...&dow=7` |
| Unix-epoch numeric seed | ✅ `?epoch=1778942730` | ❌ (dropped; web computes h/m/s) |
| Public constructor for seeded state | `new()` + `set_from_unix_seconds` | `with_initial_registers(...)` as single source of truth |
| Default | Zero ✅ | Zero ✅ |
| Battery story | Web layer owns | Web layer owns (explicit) |
| Branch name | `pr/i2c-ds1307-system-time` | `pr/ds1307-initial-time-and-system-preset` |

**Notable design choice in the brief:** the web's battery math uses `% 86400` — it only persists *time-of-day* across page-closed gaps, not date. That's why the brief skips a Unix-epoch path: date arithmetic across days isn't part of the battery semantics. Consistent.

**My concerns / questions before implementing:**

1. **`set_from_unix_seconds` — keep public, demote, or drop?** It's not on the brief's removal list (only "Rust `with_system_clock()` API" is forbidden), and it's the natural backbone for `?preset=system`. I'd keep it public but downplay it in docs — it's a "if you happen to have a Unix epoch handy" entry, while per-field setters are primary.

2. **Replace or stack on `5a92afe`?** Since the brief obsoletes most of that commit's CLI surface, I'd add a single refinement commit on top of it; if you want clean history at merge time you (or coordinator) can squash. Alternatively I can `git reset --hard 5a92afe^` and write a single fresh commit — destructive on this local branch only, no upstream impact.

3. **Branch rename.** I'd rename `pr/i2c-ds1307-system-time` → `pr/ds1307-initial-time-and-system-preset` to match the brief. No new branch.

Want me to proceed with **(stack a refinement commit, keep `set_from_unix_seconds` public, rename branch)**, or do you want **(reset and single-commit)** for cleaner history? Anything else in the brief I should push back on before I start?

1	//! `ds1307` — Maxim/Dallas DS1307 real-time clock (I2C).
2	//!
3	//! Eight BCD registers behind an auto-incrementing pointer, exactly as
4	//! the datasheet describes. The web UI's RTC panel reads/writes them
5	//! through the same bit-bang path a real master would use, so this
6	//! device mirrors the chip's protocol rather than offering a friendly
7	//! out-of-band interface.
8	//!
9	//! Pointer mapping (`pointer & 0x07`):
10	//!   - `0x00` — Seconds (00–59 BCD). Bit 7 = CH (Clock Halt) — masked
11	//!     out on writes so the emulated clock keeps ticking regardless.
12	//!   - `0x01` — Minutes (00–59 BCD).
13	//!   - `0x02` — Hours (00–23 BCD). Bit 6 = 12/24 mode; this device
14	//!     stores 24-hour format.
15	//!   - `0x03` — Day of Week (1–7 BCD).
16	//!   - `0x04` — Date (01–31 BCD).
17	//!   - `0x05` — Month (01–12 BCD).
18	//!   - `0x06` — Year (00–99 BCD).
19	//!   - `0x07` — Control. Stored verbatim; the SQW/RAM/OUT bits don't
20	//!     affect timekeeping in this emulation.
21	//!
22	//! ## Power-on default and "battery backup"
23	//!
24	//! A fresh `Ds1307Device::new(addr)` initializes every register to 0x00
25	//! — matching a real chip whose battery has never been installed: time
26	//! 00:00:00 on 00/00/00, CH bit clear, the master can read it but the
27	//! values are meaningless until the master writes the clock.
28	//!
29	//! Real DS1307 silicon keeps ticking on a coin-cell across main-power
30	//! cycles, but the chip itself has no notion of "wall clock" — its
31	//! crystal just counts oscillator ticks regardless of what year the
32	//! human at the bench thinks it is. We model this honestly:
33	//!
34	//! - The device exposes `set_from_unix_seconds(secs)` as the single
35	//!   public seed entry. It does *not* call `SystemTime::now()`
36	//!   internally — that would couple chip emulation to host wall-clock
37	//!   and break deterministic tests.
38	//! - `tick_second()` is the master-driven advance; the bus owner
39	//!   (web run-loop, CLI test, whatever) calls it once per emulated
40	//!   second.
41	//! - "Battery backup" is a *consumer-side* persistence concern. The
42	//!   web UI saves `(rtc_unix_secs, host_unix_secs)` to local storage
43	//!   on shutdown, and on next startup computes
44	//!   `current_rtc = saved_rtc + (now_host - saved_host)`, passing the
45	//!   result back through `set_from_unix_seconds`. The emulator stays
46	//!   pure; the persistence math lives where state actually persists.
47	//!
48	//! The CLI's `--i2c-device ds1307@<addr>?epoch=now` (or
49	//! `?epoch=<unix_seconds>`) is sugar for the same `set_from_unix_seconds`
50	//! path — the registry parser handles the `SystemTime::now()` call
51	//! when it sees `now`, so the host-clock dependency stays at the
52	//! consumer boundary.
53	
54	use crate::peripherals::i2c::device::{Ack, I2cDevice};
55	
56	/// Default 7-bit address for the DS1307.
57	pub const DEFAULT_ADDRESS: u8 = 0x68;
58	
59	const REG_SECONDS: usize = 0;
60	const REG_MINUTES: usize = 1;
61	const REG_HOURS: usize = 2;
62	const REG_DAY_OF_WEEK: usize = 3;
63	const REG_DATE: usize = 4;
64	const REG_MONTH: usize = 5;
65	const REG_YEAR: usize = 6;
66	const REG_CONTROL: usize = 7;
67	
68	const CH_BIT: u8 = 0x80;
69	
70	pub struct Ds1307Device {
71	    address: u8,
72	    pointer: u8,
73	    /// Byte index within the current write transaction. 0 = next byte
74	    /// is the pointer load; 1+ = data bytes for `regs[pointer]`.
75	    write_idx: u8,
76	    /// Eight BCD registers: [sec, min, hr, dow, date, month, year, ctrl].
77	    regs: [u8; 8],
78	}
79	
80	impl Ds1307Device {
81	    pub fn new(address: u8) -> Self {
82	        Self {
83	            address: address & 0x7F,
84	            pointer: 0,
85	            write_idx: 0,
86	            regs: [0; 8],
87	        }
88	    }
89	
90	    /// Set the time-of-day in 24-hour binary form. Out-of-range values
91	    /// are clamped to the chip's permitted ranges before BCD-encoding.
92	    pub fn set_time(&mut self, hour: u8, minute: u8, second: u8) {
93	        // Clear CH on every set so the clock starts ticking from this
94	        // moment regardless of what the master had written earlier.
95	        self.regs[REG_SECONDS] = int_to_bcd(second.min(59));
96	        self.regs[REG_MINUTES] = int_to_bcd(minute.min(59));
97	        self.regs[REG_HOURS] = int_to_bcd(hour.min(23)); // bit 6 stays 0 = 24-hour
98	    }
99	
100	    /// Set the calendar in binary form.
101	    pub fn set_date(&mut self, year: u8, month: u8, date: u8, day_of_week: u8) {
102	        self.regs[REG_YEAR] = int_to_bcd(year.min(99));
103	        self.regs[REG_MONTH] = int_to_bcd(month.clamp(1, 12));
104	        self.regs[REG_DATE] = int_to_bcd(date.clamp(1, 31));
105	        self.regs[REG_DAY_OF_WEEK] = int_to_bcd(day_of_week.clamp(1, 7));
106	    }
107	
108	    /// Seed the chip from a Unix epoch timestamp (UTC seconds since
109	    /// 1970-01-01). Does full leap-year math during the day→YMD
110	    /// decomposition — required to map Unix seconds back to a calendar
111	    /// date correctly. (`tick_second()` itself stays leap-year-naive
112	    /// per the original brief; the two concerns are independent.)
113	    ///
114	    /// Years map as the DS1307's two-digit form: 2000→00, 2026→26, ...,
115	    /// wrapping mod 100 past 2099.
116	    ///
117	    /// This is the only public seed entry by design. Pulling the host
118	    /// wall-clock is a consumer concern: the CLI registry does it when
119	    /// it sees `?epoch=now`; the web UI does it (and the
120	    /// battery-backed-persistence math) when restoring from local
121	    /// storage. See the module docs for the persistence pattern.
122	    pub fn set_from_unix_seconds(&mut self, secs: u64) {
123	        let (year, month, date, dow, hour, minute, second) = decompose_unix_seconds(secs);
124	        self.set_date(year, month, date, dow);
125	        self.set_time(hour, minute, second);
126	    }
127	
128	    pub fn second(&self) -> u8 {
129	        bcd_to_int(self.regs[REG_SECONDS] & !CH_BIT)
130	    }

feat(i2c): DS1307 per-field CLI params + ?preset=system

Supersedes the 5a92afe ?epoch=<...> Rust-API surface (already on
origin/main) with the device-shaped CLI grammar dcxas asked for in
docs/briefs/dcemu-ds1307-initial-time-and-system-preset.md. The CLI
gains:

  ds1307@<addr>[?hour=<n>][?minute=<n>][?second=<n>]
              [?date=<n>][?month=<n>][?year=<n>][?dow=<n>]
              [?preset=system]

Per-field params seed individual registers; preset=system reads the
host wall-clock at attach time and fills all 7 time registers.
preset and any per-field are mutually exclusive. Default (no params)
stays cold-start hardware behavior (all zeros).

Library surface:

- New `Ds1307Device::with_initial_registers(addr, [u8; 8])` is the
  single source of truth for initial register state; `new(addr)` now
  delegates with `[0; 8]`. Callers building seeded devices from Rust
  (e.g. the web panel's "battery restore" path) use this with
  BCD-encoded bytes — `int_to_bcd` and `bcd_to_int` are now public
  helpers for the encode/decode round-trip.

- `set_from_unix_seconds` is demoted from pub to pub(crate). It
  remains the backbone for `?preset=system` but is no longer a
  documented Rust entry point — per coordinator guidance, that path
  is off-pattern for both CLI users and the web panel. Library
  consumers compute the seven BCD fields themselves and pass them
  through `with_initial_registers`.

- `Ds1307HandleExt::set_from_unix_seconds` is gone for the same
  reason; the slider-driven runtime mutation path stays on
  `set_time`/`set_date` (binary integers, BCD internally).

  second 0-59, date 1-31, month 1-12, year 0-99, dow 1-7) with

- Non-decimal field values rejected with a clear "'<key>' not a

- Brief's specified six (`with_time_params`, `with_full_date`,
  `preset_system`, `preset_conflicts_with_hour`, `out_of_range`,
  `unknown_param_still_rejected`), plus two extras: `preset` in

  → address-map lookup → I2cDevice read path the brief asks for.
